original_question: Do any two sufficiently large Costas arrays necessarily share a common distance vector? More specifically, is it enough for the smaller array to have size at least 3 x 3 and the larger to have size at least 5 x 5 for a common distance vector to be forced?
target_in_paper: Problem 12 in §5.3 (“Alternative construction techniques”). The paper introduces it as the stronger statement needed in the discussion of whether block-diagonal concatenation of two Costas arrays can itself be Costas, and formulates it as asking whether any two sufficiently large Costas arrays must share a distance vector, with the suggested thresholds that the smaller array have order at least 3 and the larger order at least 5. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper-faithful target: it identifies the right object (Costas arrays), the right property (having a common distance vector), the right asymptotic flavor (“sufficiently large”), and the same suggested concrete size bounds (smaller at least 3×3, larger at least 5×5) that appear in Problem 12. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, it should define a Costas array formally: an order-n permutation array, equivalently a bijection f:[n]→[n] whose distance vectors are all distinct. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

It should define “distance vector” explicitly as a vector between two dots; in permutation notation these are the vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) for 1≤j<i≤n. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
It should make the quantifiers explicit by naming the two array orders, say n1 and n2 with n1≤n2, rather than only saying “smaller” and “larger.” ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

It should state that the problem ranges over arbitrary Costas arrays, not merely algebraically constructed ones; the paper only remarks that an earlier study treated the algebraically constructed case. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

It should preserve the paper’s exact scope: the phrase “large enough” is intentionally left informal, followed by the suggestion that n1≥3 and n2≥5 may already suffice, rather than being replaced by a stronger or different asymptotic statement. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

If one wants to retain the paper’s immediate intent, it helps to note the nearby motivation: this common-distance-vector statement is introduced because it would rule out block-diagonal concatenation as a general construction technique. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
refined_question: Let A1 and A2 be Costas arrays of orders n1 and n2, respectively, with n1≤n2. Here a distance vector means the vector between two dots of a Costas array; equivalently, if Ak corresponds to a Costas permutation fk:[nk]→[nk], its distance vectors are the pairs (i-j, fk(i)-fk(j)) with 1≤j<i≤nk. Is it true that any two sufficiently large Costas arrays must have at least one distance vector in common? More specifically, is it already enough to assume n1≥3 and n2≥5 to force A1 and A2 to share a common distance vector?
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Problem 12, not a broader concatenation problem and not a special case restricted to algebraic families. Definition 1 supplies the needed formal meaning of “distance vector” and “Costas array,” while the surrounding discussion in §5.3 explains why this question is being asked: it is the stronger statement the author says would be needed to show that concatenating two Costas arrays in block-diagonal form cannot generally yield a Costas array. No ambient field, ring, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency assumptions belong here; this is a purely combinatorial question about general Costas arrays and their distance sets. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
